title: Merge Overlapping Intervals

concept.title: Sort by start, then sweep
body: After sorting the intervals by their **start**, any interval that overlaps the previous result must overlap its *last* merged interval. So one sweep is enough: if the next start is not beyond the end of the last merged interval, extend that end (to the larger of the two ends), otherwise begin a new merged interval.
Intervals that only touch, like `[1, 3]` and `[3, 5]`, count as overlapping here. Merging intervals is the first step of many scheduling problems.

statement: You are given `n` closed intervals `[l, r]`. Merge all intervals that overlap or touch (`[1, 3]` and `[3, 5]` become `[1, 5]`). Print the number of resulting intervals, followed by the intervals sorted by their start.
inputFormat: Each of the next `n` lines has `l` and `r` with `l <= r`.
outputFormat: The first line: the number `k` of merged intervals.
hints: Sort the intervals by their start.
Compare the start of each interval with the end of the last merged one.
If it starts at or before that end, extend the end with `max`, otherwise start a new interval.

explanation: After sorting by start, each interval either extends the last merged interval or starts a new one.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
iv = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

iv.sort()
merged = []
for l, rr in iv:
    if merged and l <= merged[-1][1]:
        merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], rr)
    else:
        merged.append([l, rr])
print(len(merged))
for l, rr in merged:
    print(l, rr)
